headline: The drug was
body: Given for an unrelated tumour. It blocks FGFR signalling broadly rather than targeting one receptor. The skeletal overgrowth was an adverse effect, not the goal.
punch: Nobody was trying to make this child taller.

headline: To see why that matters
body: It's caused by a gain-of-function mutation in FGFR3. The receptor is stuck partly on, and constant FGFR3 signalling suppresses chondrocyte proliferation in the growth plate.
punch: Too much FGFR3 signal means too little growth.

headline: So the case report
body: Block FGFR broadly and you get overgrowth. The mutation that overactivates FGFR3 gives you the opposite. Same axis, opposite directions.
punch: Real human evidence for the mechanism — arrived at by accident.

headline: Which is why
body: TYRA-300 and infigratinib are purpose-built selective inhibitors — infigratinib reached a 2024 NEJM trial with a matching mouse model behind it.
punch: Both were designed from scratch to hit this exact target.

headline: And the third one
body: Meclizine — decades-old, cheap, over-the-counter for motion sickness — turned out to inhibit the same pathway. It reached Phase 2 in Japan in children with achondroplasia.
punch: A motion sickness pill and a bespoke oncology molecule aiming at the same receptor.

headline: Downstream
body: FGFR3's growth-suppressing signal is carried out by a transcription factor called Snail1 — which makes it a candidate readout for whether any of these drugs is actually working.
punch: One measurable marker for three different strategies.

headline: But be clear
body: These are therapies for a specific genetic skeletal dysplasia, tested in patients who have it. None of this is a height enhancement pathway for people without the mutation.
punch: Correcting a broken receptor is not the same as improving a working one.

headline: It's never over
body: Real mechanisms, real citations, no protocols.
